title: Looking under the lamp
hook: he lost his key inside the house but searches the street, because the light is better there

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes threw away his cup after a child beat him at living simply: less to carry. That closed week five. Today, a new week begins.

This week's teacher isn't an emperor or a philosopher. He's a fool. Or someone who looks like one. His name is Nasruddin. In Turkey he's Nasreddin Hodja; in Iran and Central Asia, Mulla Nasruddin. People have told short, funny stories about him for a long time, in many lands: at weddings, in coffee shops, to children at bedtime. Nobody knows for sure whether he was one real man. The stories belong to the people who tell them. Here's one.
screen: `A NEW KIND OF TEACHER: A FOOL.` → `TOLD IN MANY LANDS.` → `THE STORIES BELONG TO THE TELLERS.`

segments.voice: It's night. A neighbor finds Nasruddin on his hands and knees in the street, under a lamp. What have you lost, Mulla? My key, he says. So the neighbor gets down and helps. They search a long time: every stone, every crack. Nothing. Finally the neighbor asks: where exactly did you lose it? Oh, says Nasruddin, inside the house. Then why on earth are we looking out here? Because there's more light here. It's a joke, and you're allowed to laugh. That's how these stories work: first you laugh at the fool, and a few seconds later it's easy to notice he might be you. Looking where it's easy to look, not where things are, is a very human habit. Scientists even have a name for it now: the streetlight effect, studying what's easy to measure instead of what matters. People do it with bigger things than keys. Looking for peace in the next purchase, when the restlessness is somewhere inside. Looking for the fix to a relationship in a new city, when the trouble came along in the suitcase. Some Sufi teachers have told this tale as a picture of the soul, searching the bright outside world for something lost within. But the tale itself doesn't explain. Nasruddin stories rarely do. They just leave you standing in the street with the fool, both of you holding a very good lamp, and both of you knowing, now, where the key really is.
screen: `ON HIS KNEES UNDER A LAMP.` · `I LOST IT INSIDE THE HOUSE.` · `THERE'S MORE LIGHT HERE.` · `THE FOOL IS YOU.` · then, large: `SEARCH WHERE YOU LOST IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something bigger than a key that you've been searching for lately: calm, confidence, a better night's sleep, a closer friendship. Ask honestly which lamp you've been looking under, and where you actually lost it. Don't solve it; just let the answer point toward the house.
Nasruddin. A folk trickster who searches the street for a key he lost inside, because the light is better out there.
Your line: search where you lost it. A good lamp can't find what isn't there. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Persian, Mulla Nasruddin: mulla is a title for a learned man. In Turkish he is Nasreddin Hoca (Hodja), from Persian khwaja, master.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly joke about a man who can't find his keys.
what it means: we look where it's easy, not where the thing is.

what a scholar hears: Nasruddin tales circulate in Turkish, Persian, Arabic and Central Asian versions; in some tellings of this one he has lost a ring or a coin, and some Sufi teachers have read it as a teaching story.
recall: a Persian Muslim poet and scholar

notes: Nasruddin tales are traditional and paraphrased; no modern collection is quoted. Versions vary (in some, a ring or coin; in the 'streetlight effect' version, a drunk).
Whether Nasruddin was historical is debated; Turkish tradition places him in 13th-century Akşehir. Confirm phrasing.
Persian spelling ملا نصرالدین and Turkish Hoca < Persian khwāja; confirm.
The Sufi reading is attributed to 'some Sufi teachers' (popularized in the 20th century by Idries Shah, not named or quoted). A Muslim/Sufi Keeper may refine.
Nasruddin's culture is Muslim; the stories are told as folk humor, not scripture, and the script doesn't present them as religious teaching.
